item.title: Comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) streaks across the sky (annotated) - European Space Agency
item.summary: Orientation markers and a scale bar provide celestial directions and distance.] CREDIT ESA /Euclid/Euclid Consortium/ NASA , M. Pöntinen et al. 2026 ...
item.page_text:
You have already liked this page, you can only like it once!
The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet: C/2026 S1 (Euclid).
In this image sequence it moves against background stars and galaxies in three of Euclid’s VIS camera exposures captured during the Euclid Deep Field North survey.
The images were taken at 00:41:07, 00:58:53 and 01:16:39 UTC on 17 September 2026. Each image is a 560.52 second exposure, so the comet appears like a streak because it moves across the sky during the long exposure. A fuzzy atmosphere, known as a ‘coma’ in cometary terms, is seen around the object.
[ Image description : A black-and-white telescopic view of deep space shows a faint comet, labelled “C/2026 S1 (Euclid),” moving slowly against a background of stars. An arrow points to the comet’s bright central core and short tail. A timestamp updates as the animation progresses, highlighting the comet’s motion over time. Orientation markers and a scale bar provide celestial directions and distance.]

item.title: Mapped: Salary Needed to Buy a Home in 50 U.S. Cities (2026)
item.summary: Buying a median-priced home takes $492,364 a year in San Jose but $71,567 in Pittsburgh. See the salary needed to buy a home in 50 U.S. cities.
item.page_text:
A six-figure salary used to be a benchmark of financial success. In much of the U.S. housing market, it’s now closer to the starting point for buying a home, even with a substantial down payment.
This map shows the annual income needed to buy a median-priced existing home in 50 major U.S. metro areas in Q2 2026, using data from HSH.com . It assumes a 20% down payment and a 30-year fixed mortgage, with principal, interest, property taxes, and insurance taking up 28% of gross income.
California dominates the expensive end of the ranking. San Jose leads at $492.4K a year, followed by San Francisco ($368.0K), San Diego ($256.7K), and Los Angeles ($215.1K).
Outside California, New York City ($213.8K), Boston ($212.6K), and Seattle ($200.8K) are the only metros requiring annual incomes above $200K.
The table below ranks all 50 metro areas by the income needed to buy a median-priced home, along with each metro’s median home price and monthly mortgage payment:
All 12 Western metros require more than the national figure of $112.7K, while the cheaper half of the ranking consists of Southern and Midwestern metros, plus Buffalo and Pittsburgh.
In coastal California, much of what buyers pay for is the land itself. Land accounted for 59% to 68% of a single-family home’s value in the San Jose, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and San Diego metros in 2022, compared with 40% nationally and 22% in Pittsburgh, according to FHFA estimates .
Nationally, buyers needed $112.7K a year, about 29% more than the 2025 U.S. median household income of $87.5K, according to the Census Bureau .
The gap between home prices and household incomes is especially striking in San Jose. Although the typical household earns roughly twice the national median, the median home costs nearly five times as much as the national median. As a result, the typical local household earns only about one-third of the income needed to buy a median-priced home.
At the other end of the ranking, these five metros require the lowest salaries:
Based on 2024 Census data , the latest available by metro area, median household incomes in Oklahoma City and Louisville fell short of the required salaries by less than 2%.
Compared with Q2 2025, the income needed fell in 30 of the 50 metros as the average 30-year mortgage rate dropped from 6.79% to 6.41%.
However, the required income rose in 13 of the 17 Midwest and Northeast metros, led by St. Louis (+3.8%), Hartford (+3.6%), and Providence (+3.3%). Even Pittsburgh and Cleveland, the two cheapest markets, became less affordable.
New construction helps explain the regional divide. The South and West accounted for 79% of single-family housing starts in 2025, despite holding about 63% of the U.S. population, according to Census Bureau data . All 10 metros where home prices fell were also in those two regions.
The table below shows how the income needed and median home prices changed in each metro from Q2 2025 to Q2 2026:
Rising mortgage rates have since erased much of that relief. Freddie Mac’s average 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.40% in October 2026, its highest level since November 2023 and nearly a full percentage point above the Q2 average.
At that rate, buying the national median-priced home would require an annual income of approximately $122.6K, nearly $10K more than the Q2 figure. This illustrates how quickly borrowing costs can change affordability, even without a corresponding increase in home prices.
If you enjoyed today’s post, check out Years of Income Needed to Buy a Home by State on Voronoi.

Explore millennial homeownership rates across U.S. cities, from Provo’s 71% ownership rate to Los Angeles’ 69% rental rate.
For millennials, the likelihood of owning a home varies dramatically depending on where they live. In some U.S. metro areas, roughly seven in 10 millennial households own their homes. In others, nearly seven in 10 rent.
This visualization maps the U.S. metro areas where millennials are most likely to own or rent, using data from IPUMS USA and the University of Minnesota’s harmonized 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) 1-Year microdata.
The analysis covers 108 U.S. metro areas with at least 50,000 millennial households, comparing ownership and rental rates rather than the total number of homeowners or renters.
Utah claims the top two spots for millennial homeownership. In Provo, 71.0% of millennial households own their homes, followed by nearby Ogden at 68.9%. Grand Rapids, Michigan, ranks third at 68.1%.
Utah’s high millennial homeownership rates may partly reflect the state’s tendency toward earlier marriage and family formation, alongside strong employment growth.
Historically more attainable housing prices in places like Ogden may also have helped younger households enter the market. However, rising home prices and elevated mortgage rates have made buying increasingly difficult for prospective homeowners.
Other high-ranking metros include Lancaster, Pennsylvania (65.5%), Minneapolis, Minnesota (65.3%), and Des Moines, Iowa (63.5%), highlighting a strong showing across parts of the Midwest.
These markets contrast sharply with rental-heavy coastal metros, although local incomes, household composition, and the timing of home purchases can also shape homeownership rates .
Los Angeles is nearly the mirror image of Provo. While roughly seven in 10 millennial households own their homes in Provo, nearly seven in 10 rent in Los Angeles (69.2%).
San Jose follows with a 63.7% rental rate, while New York and Urban Honolulu are tied at 62.9%.
